meta.scale: raw EditLens score in [0, 1], 0 = human, 1 = AI; no thresholds are published
meta.note: score_alone is for one sentence as a text of its own (noisy: the model trained on 75+ words); contribution = paragraph score minus the score of the paragraph without that sentence (paragraphs of 40+ words only)

sentences.sentence: We trained a small JEPA world model in the LeWorldModel recipe for $3.30 of rented GPU time, on teleoperated demonstrations of one tabletop task on an SO-101 arm.
On this model we then re-tested the uses of such models that recent papers propose, each with a threshold written into a public register.

On policy rollouts the model never saw, a linear probe on the encoder's last-frame latent separates success from failure about as well as a hand-built colour judge, and better than a frozen DINOv2 encoder or the commanded joints.
The predictor adds nothing to this.
At the grasp the imagined latent reads the outcome at 0.70 and the current latent at 0.82, and every use that needs the predictor to roll forward misses its threshold at this data scale.
The controls are exploratory and come from one rig and one model.
LeWorldModel (LeWM) [1] trains a world model in two parts.
The encoder maps camera frames to a latent vector, and the predictor takes the current latent and a sequence of actions and imagines the latents that follow.
Both are trained together from pixels with a joint-embedding predictive (JEPA) loss.
Most of the uses proposed for these models need the predictor.

One ranks a policy's candidate action chunks by their imagined outcome, and others flag a failure when the observed latent drifts from the predicted one, read the outcome of a grasp before it happens, or plan over several time scales.
Each paper reports the use that worked on its own robot and data.
We had one such model, trained on our own arm, and ran every use we could find on it.
Each re-test is a row of a register with a threshold, a dataset, a result and a verdict.
Where we managed it, the threshold and the decision rule went into the repository before the result existed, which is all we mean by pre-registration.
All 20 rows match a pre-registration record in the commit history.
In 19 of them the bar was in place before the result, and the two-level hierarchical progress use had it in the same commit.
One more row is not a use of our model, since it times the pretrained RoboJEPA [2] and V-JEPA 2.1 [3] encoders on our on-board computer.
14 of the 20 rows fail or are no-go (Table 1).
The first draft of this paper argued something else.
We had read the failures as a sign that the latent mostly encodes the arm's pose, in which case a frozen image encoder or the commanded joints would do at least as well in each use.
Before writing it up we ran these controls on 69 policy rollouts, and the encoder read how the episode went better than either of them.
We rewrote the claim around the predictor.
We come back several times to one moment, the grasp anchor, 15 frames before the gripper first closes.
There the current latent reads the outcome at 0.82 and the imagined latent at 0.70.
The controls came after the data.
Each readout is a linear probe with leave-one-session-out (LOSO) cross-validation on the 69 rollouts (44 success, 25 failure, 13 sessions), scored against labels the author gave at rest.
The model was trained on teleoperation only and never saw these rollouts.
Because no threshold was committed for these comparisons, everything this paper says about the split between encoder and predictor is exploratory.
3 of the 3 register passes have their bar committed before the result, and the register still marks the outcome-readout verdict as retrospective.
The robot is one SO-101 arm [4] driven through LeRobot [5], with a top and a wrist camera, and the task is to put a bowl into another bowl.
We trained our model on X, split by grid layout into 157 training and 25 validation episodes.
The evaluation rollouts come from a separate dataset, X, which holds SmolVLA [6] runs recorded after our model was trained.
Our model follows the LeWM recipe [1], with a multi-view ViT encoder, an action-conditioned predictor and the SIGReg regulariser.
We compare it with four cheaper signals.
The frozen DINOv2-S control is a frozen DINOv2 small encoder [7], mean-pooled over the top and wrist views as in DINO-WM [8], and the joints control is the commanded joint vector.
The colour judge is a hand-built rule on the final frame with no learning.
Policy identity is the checkpoint that ran the episode.
In October we found a loading bug.

A timing test on the on-board computer loaded our checkpoint with X, and under the transformers version on that image (5.5.4) 192 encoder tensors did not match and were dropped without an error, so the test timed a random encoder.
We voided its latents and traced how every other use loaded the model: 26 ran the trained model and 1 ran a random one (that test).
The world-model block of VLA-JEPA, which one diagnostic below uses, loads all 351 of its keys.
Table 1 lists the 20 uses.
The takes column says what each one needs from our model: the encoder alone (7), the predictor (8) or both (5).
Among the encoder uses, reading the outcome works.
The outcome readout at rest passes, and at the grasp anchor the current latent reads the grasp at 0.82.
Reading progress does not work.

Four uses ask the latent for progress or task stage (progress monotonicity, two-level hierarchical progress [10], the latent stage tracker and SURVEYOR's latent-distance scale [13]), and all four fail.
We also ran the pose probes of LeJEPA [12], where a linear readout recovers about half of the joint variance from our encoder (R² 0.565) and more from the frozen DINOv2-S control (0.867).
The predictor does predict its own latent: at K = 30 its open-loop error is 0.31, against 0.89 for copying the last latent.
The uses of this prediction fail.
In chunk ranking [1] the model puts the executed chunk first in 0.60 of anchors, below the threshold of 0.8, while the commanded actions alone reach 0.68–0.90.
The surprise monitor catches 2/8 at 2/42 failures.
The hierarchical planner [14], the conformal surprise band, re-ranking, the risk head [11] and the calibrated reflex also miss their thresholds, by the margins in Table 1.
We tested whether the encoder carries anything that a frozen encoder or the joints do not, by setting our model beside the four other signals on the same 69 rollouts (Table 2).
Every probe is a LOSO linear probe against the author's labels.

At rest the interval is a 95 % episode-bootstrap CI, and at the anchor it is a bootstrap of the mean over 5 seeds of the out-of-fold AUROC, with episodes resampled jointly across the seeds (2,000 resamples, percentile).
At rest our model is level with the colour judge, whose CI overlaps its own, and above the frozen encoder and the joints.
At the grasp anchor no judge applies, and our model is above both controls.
The pose probes hold the joints better than our encoder does and the outcome worse, so on these rollouts the encoder has outcome information that the pose alone does not give.
The anchor column depends on how the five seeds are combined.
If we average the predictions before scoring, our model gets 0.8377, frozen DINOv2-S 0.7175 and the joints 0.5346.
Seed 0 alone gives 0.7554, 0.7024 and 0.5574, with a smaller gap to the frozen encoder.
The order is the same.
On SURVEYOR's scale check the controls do better than our model.
Frozen DINOv2-S (τ 0.3601) and the joints (τ 0.0265) pass, and our model fails with τ 1.2488, where SURVEYOR reports 0.20.
The task and the rollouts are the same for all three features, so we take the failure as a property of our latent space.
The register's own outcome-readout row reports 1.000, but that number was scored against the colour judge's labels on 87 rollouts.
Against the author's labels on the 69 rollouts, the same readout gives 0.9545.
ContactGuard [9] finds that probes on the imagined latent beat probes on the current latent for grasp tasks, and we expected the same at our grasp anchor.
The pre-registered threshold asked the imagined latent for ≥ 0.85, ≥ +0.05 over the current one.
We find the reverse.
With the same encoder and the same anchor, the current latent reads the outcome at 0.82 and the imagined latent at 0.70, so the row fails.
We also ran the distillation probe on our model's inverse-dynamics term, pooled over the 25 teleoperation validation episodes.
The trained model scores 0.7476 and its random initialisation 0.7974, a difference of −0.0499 with a 95 % paired episode-bootstrap CI of [−0.7403, +0.6559] (X).
The term also depends on the machine.
The same untrained network scored 1.4383 on one machine and 0.7974 and 0.8042 on two others, because it is sensitive to the BLAS library and to ridge conditioning.
The surprise monitor has a failure-class AUROC of 0.775, below its sanity bar, so we checked it for a loading or scoring bug.
The same scorer reproduces the open-loop corruption ratios at K = 30 (X): cross-episode gives 3.428 against 3.341 in the original run, and constant-first 2.558 against 2.543.
We found no bug.
We ran an action-shuffle check on the predictor of VLA-JEPA at 5 anchors (Table 3, from X).
Action tokens from another episode differ from the true ones by 21–28 % in relative L2, yet they move the loss by about 0.05 %, and zeroing the tokens moves it by about 1.05 % on average.
The forward pass is deterministic.
The predictor barely uses its actions, and with a failure-class AUROC of 0.501, below the same sanity check, we leave its table unread under the frozen bar.
One pass in the register uses the imagined latent: in the anticipation step of the outcome-readout gate, it beat policy identity by +0.179.
That bar is retrospective.
We reran the same idea twice with the threshold committed first, in the grasp probe and in the calibrated surprise reflex, and both fail.
LeWorldModel [1] trains the recipe we use end to end from pixels and plans with it in Push-T and in simulation.
We tested its two planning uses on our arm, and both fail.
LeJEPA's identifiability analysis [12] predicts that SIGReg latents identify the state up to anisotropy, which our pose probes support in part.
DINO-WM [8] plans on frozen DINOv2 [7] patches, and our frozen control uses the same design.
We timed V-JEPA 2.1 [3] and RoboJEPA [2] on our on-board computer, and both are too slow.
ContactGuard [9] finds imagined-latent probes better than current-latent ones on grasp tasks, and on our arm we find the reverse.
ReAP's action-conditioned risk [11], the hierarchical planners of HWM [14] and H-JEPA [10], and SURVEYOR's latent-distance scale [13] also miss here, at this data scale.

SaiVLA-JEPA [15] reports that a training-only future-latent head adds +0.03 points to control on 10,030 paired episodes, and HIJP [16] finds LeWM below goal-conditioned behaviour cloning in simulation.
The split between encoder and predictor is exploratory.
We chose its probes after the data and fit them on 69 rollouts labelled by a single operator, the author.
The model never saw these rollouts, and every probe is cross-validated by session.
A fresh set of rollouts scored under a threshold committed first would confirm or reject the split, and that needs a day on the arm.
All results come from one model at one data scale, and a second point at 653 episodes is costed and queued.

We did not run three controls, because the surprise monitor and the imagined arm of the grasp probe would each need a predictor trained on frozen DINOv2-S features or on the joints, and progress monotonicity with the controls would need a reimplementation.
In the register the outcome-readout verdict is retrospective, and the two-level hierarchical progress use has its bar in the same commit as its result.
Ordered by commit alone, without the audit, the register reads 13 bar-first and 6 same-commit rows.
We tested 20 published uses on a $3.30 world model.
At this data scale the encoder reads the outcome, and the predictor adds nothing to that reading.
In chunk ranking the commanded actions did better than the predictor, so they are worth keeping as a baseline for any model of this size.

Read the takes column against the verdict: the predictor uses fail.
Bar, result and verdict are quoted from repro/register/expected/FEASIBILITY.md §2.

We re-tested the central claims of recent robot-learning papers on an SO-101 arm with a Jetson Orin NX, a rig whose parts cost €1,350, for $45.10 of compute.
Each re-test ran the cheapest baseline first, with its pass mark committed before the run, and every published number rebuilds from stored rows.
Of the 37 paper claims we tested, 12 held on this hardware.
We sort the failures into three proposed classes, named after the condition a claim did not survive.
One is the clock, where a method misses the real-time budget on the edge GPU.
The other two cover zero-shot judges beaten by a trivial signal and latent planners beaten by the commanded joints.
A blind second reader still has to confirm the classes.
We also audited our own pre-registration by commit ancestry, which shows the order of bar and result for most gates and not for the rest.
Most of the 22 papers in this study were shown on setups far from ours: 9 in simulation and 7 on rigs above X5k, which is where our rig falls.
The appendix table gives the rig of each paper, including the 3 in between and the 1 that does not say.
Our rig is an SO-101 arm and a Jetson Orin NX 16 GB, and the parts with a stated price cost €1,350 (2 small parts are not priced yet).
The register grew out of our own write-ups, 29 so far, each published with its data.
This paper collects them in one table and audits how the table was kept.
Here is one entry.
An adaptive chunking paper claims that choosing the chunk length from the entropy of sampled chunks follows the task's phases, long in transport and short at the grasp.
On our edge GPU one such decision takes 4,751 ms, and the budget is 298 ms.
The entry records a fail on this rig, which says nothing about the method on the hardware it was shown on.
Next to the verdict it keeps the claim in the paper's words, our pass mark, our measurement and the published rows.
For each claim we first run, on the same rows, the cheapest signal the learned model has to beat: copy-last for a predictor, the commanded joints for a latent and episode length for a judge.
The pass mark is committed before the run, and §2 checks how often that held.
We chose the papers for the stack this rig runs (world models, VLA policies, failure monitors, chunking, edge latency) and entered each one in the register before its test.
The register file lists the papers scheduled next.
A gate's pass mark had to be in version control before its result.
Notes and commit dates can be edited by hand, but commit ancestry cannot be changed without rewriting history that others have already cloned.
We therefore order each gate with X, between the first commit that contains its bar and the first commit that contains its result.
Table 1 gives the classes for the 89 gates logged by 2026-10-31.
Most are bar-first, and 0 are result-first.
A same-commit gate is one where bar and result entered the repository together, which says nothing about which was written first.

Our first pass used text search and found 31 same-commit gates, mostly because of batch logging: a bar written earlier in a protocol, plan, scorer or specification often reached the log in the same commit as its result.
We traced each same-commit gate back to that file.
This moved 21 gates to bar-first and 4 to no-bar (their bar cell declares none), and 6 stayed same-commit.
The audit table in the repository gives the evidence line for every move.
We did not re-audit the gates that were already bar-first.
One open candidate remains, the reward-model progress test of 2026-11-01, which is same-commit by text search although its protocol (X) is older than the log commit.
The early gates mixed point estimates and different intervals, so we recomputed 10 of them from stored rows with one statistic, the episode bootstrap (2,000 resamples, percentile 95 % CI).
For 3 of them the bar falls inside the interval (Table 2).
The colour judge is a fail on the point estimate, and its interval does not settle it.
The false-intervention threshold was fitted to meet its rate, so that interval is only descriptive.
The register keeps the pre-registered point verdicts and marks these three as fragile.
All 29 write-ups rebuild from their published rows.
We also reran gates cold, from a fresh clone with no credentials, and 6 reran and matched, 5 of them exactly.
12 more stop at the world-model environment, which is not published yet, and publishing it would unblock most of them.
The remaining 11 need a larger GPU, a private checkpoint, the arm or a step the write-up leaves out.
We checked the register's citations and paper-side fields against the papers' PDFs and corrected them.
Of the 38 arXiv ids the register names, the ones missing from our papers mirror all belong to scheduled tests, and the one tested paper with no arXiv id was not checked against a PDF.
Table 3 counts the verdicts by paper and by claim row, and the appendix lists every entry.
On claims taken from papers, 12 of 37 reproduce and 18 fail.
The other 8 rows test our own baselines, for example that the commanded joints beat the world model, and 5 of those hold.
The adaptive chunking entry of §1 misses the real-time budget on the edge GPU, with one decision taking 4,751 ms against 298 ms.
The method may work on faster hardware.
We call this kind of failure class A, the clock.
In other entries a model judged outcomes without training on this rig.
A learned reward model detects failures at AUROC 0.818, and episode length alone reaches 0.938.

Judges of success, failure or progress that lose to a trivial signal like this form class B. Class C is about learned latents used to plan, rank or track progress that lose to the joints, to copy-last or to an action-only baseline.
A world model, for example, ranks the executed chunk first in 0.60 of anchors, where its pass mark was 0.8 and an action-only baseline reaches 0.68–0.90.
These examples illustrate the classes and do not count them.
Under a protocol committed before any labelling, the labels count only once a blind second reader labels the same 20 failed rows on the same form and agrees with the first reading at Cohen's κ ≥ 0.6.
That reading has not happened yet.
One operator, the author, ran the rig and labelled the outcomes, at rest and not always blind to the arm, so observer bias is the main confound.
Where commit order shows it, the pass mark predates the run and a label could not move the bar.
A blind two-reader protocol for the failure classes is committed but has not run, so no verdict has a second reader yet.
For 29 of the 89 gates the repository cannot show whether bar or result came first, and 21 of the bar-first verdicts rest on matching a bar text in an earlier file.
Under the bootstrap 3 verdicts are fragile.
Cold reruns cover 6 gates so far, and the unpublished world-model environment blocks most of the rest.
A failure here describes this rig, not the paper in its own setting.
Because the papers were chosen for one stack, the rate describes this register and not the field.

Two works use the same arm to evaluate policies: a standardized real-world benchmark that reports a taxonomy of failures and recoveries for VLA policies [arXiv:2606.08881], and a fleet of SO-101 cells that evaluates policies at scale [arXiv:2607.24481].
The vla-eval tool runs VLAs across 14 simulation benchmarks [arXiv:2603.13966].
A benchmark of demonstration quality studies one method family [arXiv:2610.18869].
We test the claims behind methods (judges, world models, latency) against thresholds fixed before the run, and we audit our own pre-registration.
RoboSeed [arXiv:2610.40026] is the closest work.

It scores VLA and world-action models on five dimensions, including reproduction evidence and deployment affordability, and its reproduction-evidence score counts five audit milestones (configuration mapping, task records, task coverage, training records, seeds).
Its authors state that this score is not a probability that a result is correct.
We give one pass or fail per claim on a €1,350 rig.
We re-tested 37 paper claims on a €1,350 rig, and 12 held.
The compute cost $45.10, and every row behind the verdicts is published.
Our own history cannot show the order of bar and result for 29 of 89 gates.
If you re-test a paper on a cheap rig, run its cheapest baseline on the same rows first and commit the threshold before the run.
Every number here can be rebuilt from the repository (X).

Reward models that score robot rollouts are also used as failure detectors, and we compared two zero-shot reward models with plain episode length.
On ArmnetBench, a public SO-101 benchmark where runs end at a time limit, length separates failure from success at AUROC 0.942 within policy.
Failed runs there are slow rather than cut off, and length observed only up to half of the longest episode still gives 0.851.
Both reward models score below length, the better one at 0.821.
On our own rollouts, which an operator stopped by judgment, length falls to 0.56 and neither reward model beats the identity of the policy.
A judge that sees the finished episode passes its threshold there, at an operating point chosen in-sample, and no mid-episode monitor reaches its bar.
The baseline a detector has to beat depends on the dataset's stopping rule.
Papers that evaluate a reward model as a failure detector usually compare it with other learned detectors.
When a benchmark stops failed runs at a time limit, the length of an episode also encodes its outcome, and so can the identity of the policy that ran (we call this the policy-identity null).
When an operator stops each run by judgment, both signals are weaker.
We call the way a dataset ends its episodes its *stopping rule*.
None of the reward-model papers in our library reports the stopping rule or a length baseline.

We started with a narrower claim, that elapsed time is the reward model to beat, and our own rollouts did not support it: on them length is near chance, and a robot-trained judge passed its pre-registered threshold.
The stopping rule separates the two results, so it became the subject of the paper.
We measured length on ArmnetBench and on our own rollouts, with the length analyses frozen before any number existed.
We compared it with two zero-shot reward models, Robometer and TOPReward, and on our 88 operator-stopped rollouts also with every judge and monitor we had run.
ArmnetBench v0.1 has 8 tasks and 7 policies on the SO-101.
We use its 2,047 policy rollouts with a success or failure class (515 successes, 1,532 failures) and leave out the teleoperated episodes.
One task, pushing a Displayport cable (270 rollouts), has rollouts of a single class and so no per-task AUROC.
Our own data are 88 labelled bowls-task episodes on one SO-101 arm with a Jetson Orin NX, and every monitor gate used the same 50-episode subset (42 successes, 8 failures).
The author was the operator, who stopped each run and labelled it at rest, not blind to the policy.
On ArmnetBench, episode length is a strong failure detector within each policy (Table 1, Fig. 1).
Pooled over policies it reaches 0.938, and within each policy it ranges from 0.91 to 0.96.
Pair-weighted, the within-policy value is 0.942, with a CI of 0.927–0.956.
We ran Robometer-4B zero-shot, as its authors ship it, and it scores 0.818 pooled and 0.821 within policy.
The within-policy value is pair-weighted over its per-policy scores, whose range stands in for a CI (§7).
TOPReward, run with Qwen3-VL-8B and no training, scores 0.661 within policy, and its paired difference to length has a 95 % CI of -0.31 to -0.25.
The protocols fixed each model's primary score before any score existed: the success probability for Robometer and the success score of its paper for TOPReward.
Two other scores from the same runs, listed in Table 1 as descriptive rows, are higher and still below length.

Robometer scales a general-purpose reward model through trajectory comparisons, and TOPReward reads the token probabilities of a video-language model as hidden rewards.
A survey of verifiers for robot policies covers the wider family.
FAIL-Detect and SAFE learn uncertainty- and feature-based failure scores for imitation and VLA policies.
FARM reads failure signals from the internal states of a frozen world model, as our world-model monitors do, and our risk head follows ReAP, which predicts action-conditioned risk.
VLA-Corrector verifies stages, Spotter adds a reflecting VLM, and REMORA tracks progress through errors and recovery.
ArmnetBench and a standardized SO-101 VLA benchmark evaluate policies on the same arm.
None of these works reports the elapsed-length baseline under the dataset's stopping rule.
The judge pass on our own rollouts rests on 8 failures and on operating thresholds chosen on the same 50 episodes, which a single operator, the author, labelled without being blind to the policy.
The threshold-free AUROCs do not depend on the threshold, and fresh rollouts scored at the frozen thresholds would confirm the operating points.
17 of the 25 failures in our 69 rollouts are TurboVLA's, so any score that reads the policy gets the policy-identity null for free.
The risk head is trained and tested on the same 50 episodes, with five folds by episode that keep episodes from leaking (tasks and policies do leak).
Robometer's per-episode scores stayed on an older machine.
Its within-policy number therefore has no episode-bootstrap CI and it is missing from the truncation analysis, and a copy from that machine or a re-score of about $6 would restore both.
TOPReward's paper does not give its prefix count, frames per query or Yes/No wording, so those are our choices.
The ArmnetBench result covers eight tasks, and the timeout is approximated by each task's longest episode.
On ArmnetBench, where runs end at a time limit, episode length beat both reward models.
On our operator-stopped rollouts length was at chance, and a judge that saw the whole finished episode caught the failures.
When you evaluate a reward model as a failure detector, report episode length within policy on the same rows and say how the episodes ended.

Length observed up to a fraction of the task's longest episode, AUROC within policy: most of the signal is there by half the episode (band: 95 % CI).

We re-measured seven training-free methods for action chunking in flow-matching VLAs, whose papers report numbers from desktop GPUs, on the hardware a low-cost robot runs: SmolVLA on a Jetson Orin NX.
All tests share one checkpoint and the same recorded episodes, each had its threshold committed before the run, and every number traces to a result file and a protocol commit.
On this board the vision encoder takes 151.0 of 219.0 ms of server time per chunk (25 W).
The two methods that act on the seam between chunks pass.
A gradient-free prefix overwrite cuts the boundary jump by 72 % or more, and movement-primitive seam conditioning removes most of the seam jerk.
The sampling methods do not transfer, because vla.cpp samples in sequence and every N-sample method pays for N chunks one after another.
Several training-free chunking tricks for flow-matching VLAs were published this year, with numbers from desktop and data-centre GPUs (RTX 4090, A100, H100, RTX 5090).
There a chunk costs tens of milliseconds, and spare compute can hide an extra pass.
A robot people can buy runs its policy on an edge GPU, where most of the chunk goes to the vision encoder, which these tricks do not touch.
We measured how much of each trick is left on such a board.
Our robot is an SO-101 arm [arXiv:2606.08881] with a Jetson Orin NX 16 GB.
It runs SmolVLA [arXiv:2506.01844] through vla.cpp, a C++ inference engine, on episodes recorded with LeRobot.
This paper started once SmolVLA ran on the arm through vla.cpp, when we looked at where the rest of a chunk's time went and at which published tricks could still help.
We took seven of them, each as a gate with a bar committed before the number.
Offline effects get an episode bootstrap, and latencies are medians of at least 50 calls.
The appendix maps every number to its result file and protocol commit.
We follow one chunk of ten Euler steps at full power (MAXN_SUPER), which costs 237.5 ms end to end (Fig. 1).
Vision takes 150.7 ms, prefill 14.9 ms, and each denoise step 5.3 ms.
At 25 W the server-side split is 151.0 ms of vision in 219.0 ms.
A trick that only touches the denoising loop works on at most a quarter of the chunk.
Two power modes appear in this paper because each gate's protocol froze the mode it ran in: the serving split and the boundary experiments ran at 25 W, and the latency experiments at full power.
Every number below carries its mode.
All offline effects use the same SmolVLA checkpoint and the same 20 recorded episodes, with 254 chunk boundaries per delay.
Table 1 gives every effect, bar and verdict.
Two tricks act on the seam between chunks, and both pass.
The first overwrites the new chunk's executed prefix with the actions already committed, and it passes the 50 % jump-cut bar at every delay, in PyTorch and in vla.cpp, where it adds 0.4 ms per chunk.
The second is movement-primitive chunking [arXiv:2610.39451].
Projecting each chunk onto ten Gaussian bases keeps the error within its bar and removes within-chunk jerk.
Conditioning on the last action sent removes 83–87 % of the seam jerk at +0.19° of error, against 73–84 % in its paper (we measured on the commanded stream only).
Exact real-time chunking [arXiv:2506.07339] inpaints the prefix with guidance instead of overwriting it.
It cuts the jump by less than 50 % at every delay (Fig. 2), and in PyTorch it costs 1.9× a naive chunk.
Cutting the Euler steps from ten to two [arXiv:2610.32102] saves 41 ms per chunk at full power, which is small next to the vision cost.
The paper claims that the action cloud contracts around an unchanged centroid, with a cloud ratio of 0.51 on π0.
Our ratio is 0.78, between the bar of 0.70 and the fail line of 0.85, so the claim is not proven here.
The paper also expects fewer steps to remove edge-GPU thermal throttling, and our Orin did not throttle at ten steps in either power mode.
We keep ten steps, as the protocol says while the contraction is unproven.
Two tricks sample several chunks per decision.
Speculative chunk selection [arXiv:2610.28019] samples four candidates and uses the pre-commit frame to pick the one closest to the recorded teleoperation continuation.
Offline it beats a random pick (one continuation per frame, training-set episodes, open loop).
Its paper promises no added control-step delay, but on the Orin vla.cpp samples the candidates in sequence, and a cycle costs 1,200 ms and 37 control ticks against 8 for a naive chunk (Fig. 3).
Entropy-adaptive chunk length [arXiv:2604.04161] samples 20 chunks per decision, and one decision takes 4,751 ms on the Orin against a threshold of 298 ms.
Its chosen length also sits at the floor in both task phases, and the jump is no better than with fixed chunks and the overwrite.
The prefix overwrite and the primitive projection with seam conditioning act on the seam, and each costs under a millisecond on this board.
We keep ten Euler steps until the contraction passes its threshold, since the two-step saving is small next to vision.
Exact guidance, speculative selection and adaptive length all pay for N chunks in series on a sequential engine.
If you run one of them on an edge board, check first whether your engine samples in a batch, because ours does not.
This version is offline and latency only, and the closed-loop columns on the arm, for seam smoothing and for the overwrite in the robot client, belong to a longer version.

Other chunking tricks are also reported on desktop-class GPUs, and we did not re-measure them here: extending the executing chunk instead of resampling [arXiv:2610.05719], driving reactive chunking with a latent world model [arXiv:2606.18589], and fine-tuning the policy for latency with reinforcement learning [arXiv:2608.23831].
On the engine side, TurboVLA [arXiv:2607.27205] pushes VLA throughput on a desktop GPU. vla.cpp, the engine we measure, runs VLAs on edge boards.

Two works use the same arm to evaluate policies, a standardized benchmark that reports failures and recoveries of VLA policies [arXiv:2606.08881] and a fleet of SO-101 cells that evaluates policies at scale [arXiv:2607.24481].
We re-measure the execution tricks around one policy, under bars fixed before the run.
The sampling result depends on the engine. vla.cpp samples sequentially, and we contribute to it (the overwrite runs on our fork, X).
Parity and determinism checks against PyTorch on the same board are in the gate logs, and a batched sampler would test the sampling result, but we have not run one.
Effects other than latency are offline and come from 20 recorded demonstrations of one task family (bowls), which the policy was trained on.
The arm gates for seam smoothing and for the overwrite in the robot client have not run.
We left out the adaptive-length arm gate because SmolVLA is at ceiling on this task, so a gain could not show.
Latency rows run at MAXN_SUPER and the serving and boundary rows at 25 W, which makes power mode a confound wherever the two are compared.
The study covers one policy, SmolVLA at 450M, since π0-class models do not fit on the Orin.
